endorsements.quote: The system should be restricted to teaching, clearly labeled as simulated, watched by an educator, and blocked from unsupervised clinical advice.

Accordingly, educators should compare general-purpose and specialized models against an expert-annotated reference set before deployment and should display source provenance, uncertainty, and the date of guideline retrieval whenever feasible [ 8 , 10 ].
Systems should therefore undergo subgroup validation and continuous monitoring.

Educational datasets should not be assembled from electronic health records without appropriate institutional approval, deidentification, data use agreements, and safeguards against reidentification [ 8 , 10 , 17 , 39 ].

unlisted_practices: Conduct prospective randomized controlled trials of LLM- and metaverse-based educational tools measuring validated outcomes including transfer of learning to supervised clinical practice.
Require learners to make an initial independent assessment before viewing AI suggestions, explain disagreements with the system, and complete periodic no-AI assessments to prevent deskilling.
Keep human educators responsible for approving cases, supervising AI use, evaluating performance, and remaining accountable for educational decisions.
Have AI agents escalate uncertain or unsafe outputs to a human educator and record the information used to generate answers.
Restrict general-purpose LLMs to low-risk uses and use constrained, expert-validated systems for higher-risk diagnostic and assessment tasks.
Calibrate haptic simulators against expert-defined task requirements and report haptic fidelity separately from visual fidelity in validation studies.
Include controlled variability and realistic clinical dilemmas in AI-generated educational cases rather than only idealized pathways.
Align educational AI and XR tools with defined clinical competencies and implement them in a staged, competency-based framework.
